periods.activity_title: Reading Harvest Hymn Aloud and Exploring Stanza Meanings

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.176): match stanza numbers to given main ideas.
Let us discuss (p.176): fill blanks on setting, tone, and capitalisation.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud from p.173–175, modelling the shift in voices — men, women, all voices. Students follow in their textbooks and note any unfamiliar words.
Draw attention to the four stanzas and their distinct speakers. Students match each of the four given main-idea sentences to its correct stanza number and share answers with the class.

Guide students through the three fill-in-the-blank questions on setting, tone, and the significance of capitalised 'Hands', 'Heart' and 'Home'. Discuss each answer briefly as a class to confirm understanding.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem is structured as a choral hymn with three elemental deities addressed in sequence — Surya, Varuna, Prithvi — before a concluding address to Brahma; keeping that architecture visible helps students match stanza ideas accurately. A common confusion is treating all four stanzas as addressed to the same deity — prompt students to identify the deity's name in each stanza. Students who find the archaic pronouns (thee, thine, thou) difficult may be directed to treat them as 'you/your' equivalents.

periods.activity_title: Literary Devices and Symbolism in the Hymn

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.177): identify poetic devices in two given lines.
Let us think and reflect (p.177): match lines to expressions and name poetic device.
Let us think and reflect (p.177): match symbols — Prithvi, Surya, Varuna — to meanings.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.177): find word/phrase repetitions in the poem and note the poet's purpose.

time_bands.activity: Revisit the poem's three elemental deities briefly. Introduce the concept of poetic devices: alliteration, personification, and metaphor, with one quick example from outside the poem.

Students identify the poetic device in 'Bright and munificent lord of the morn!' and 'We bring thee our lives and our labours for tribute' individually, then compare answers with a partner before class discussion.

Students work through the three-row matching table — pairing lines from the poem with their expressions and naming the device (imagery, metaphor, personification) from the box. Discuss the 'Seed and Scythe' metaphor in depth.
Students match the three symbols — Prithvi, Surya, Varuna — to their respective symbolic meanings and share justifications aloud. Assign the repetition task as a quick self-study exercise for home.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the poem aloud and identified its four-stanza structure, students are ready to examine how Naidu achieves her devotional tone through literary craft. The personification of Earth as 'sweet and omnipotent mother' is especially rich — encourage students to connect it to the women's voices stanza specifically. Unanchored task: the repetition-and-purpose task is assigned as self-study; students who explore it may share observations informally.

periods.activity_title: Close Reading: Extract Analysis and Short-Answer Questions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.178): four questions on Extract 1 — Surya stanza.
Let us think and reflect (p.178–179): four questions on Extract 2 — Brahma stanza.

time_bands.activity: Students locate and re-read Extract 1 (the Surya stanza, p.173) silently. Teacher reads it aloud once to re-establish the rhythmic quality of the lines.

Work through the four Extract 1 questions as a guided class discussion: the MCQ on tribute, the fill-in on 'gold', the short answer on 'mellowing radiance', and the fill-in on cymbal and flute. Establish correct answers through student responses.
Students locate and re-read Extract 2 (the Brahma stanza, p.175) silently, paying attention to 'Seed and Scythe' and the chorus stage direction 'All Voices'.

Work through the four Extract 2 questions: the MCQ on 'being', the true/false on 'Seed and Scythe', the phrase-identification SCR, and the question on how we know the lines are a chorus. Consolidate answers through class discussion.

periods.teacher_notes: Having examined the poem's literary devices, students now apply close reading to specific extracts. A common difficulty is the MCQ on 'Lord of our being' — students may conflate 'being' with physical body; prompt them to consider the scope of 'Lord of the Universe' immediately preceding it. The true/false on 'Seed and Scythe' benefits from re-reading the final stanza in full — students who only skim may miss how the metaphor completes the creation-to-harvest cycle.

periods.activity_title: Farming Implements, Poem Vocabulary, and Archaic Words

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.180): match farming-implement pictures to uses and complete names.
Let us learn (p.180–181): choose synonyms for underlined poem words from given box.
Let us learn (p.181): use a dictionary to find modern equivalents for five archaic words.

time_bands.activity: Students examine the farming-implement matching task. They match each picture to the correct use description and fill in the missing letters to complete each implement name. Teacher confirms answers and clarifies any implement unfamiliar to urban students.

Students read each sentence containing an underlined word — munificent, succour, radiance, ineffable — locate context clues, and circle them before choosing the correct synonym from the box. Discuss how context clues make dictionary lookup faster.

Students open their dictionaries (or use a class set) and look up the five archaic words: morrow, hither, quoth, betwixt, yonder. They write the modern equivalent for each. A quick whole-class comparison follows to confirm findings.

periods.teacher_notes: The vocabulary tasks move from the concrete (implement names with images) to the abstract (synonym inference and archaic-word lookup), which scaffolds student confidence. Students may conflate 'munificent' and 'beneficent' — remind them that the example sentence already establishes 'beneficent = kind', so munificent must be the remaining synonym 'generous'. The archaic-word task requires dictionaries; confirm availability before the sitting.

periods.activity_title: Listening to Paddy Cultivation and Speaking About Harvest Dishes

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.181): number seven paddy-cultivation events in correct order.
Let us listen (p.181–182): choose correct option for three comprehension questions.
Let us speak (p.182): say silent-letter words — hymn, womb, bomb — aloud.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the listening context: a talk on how paddy — the grain celebrated in the poem — is actually cultivated, from soil preparation to the market. Students receive the seven events list and read it once before listening begins.

Teacher reads the paddy-cultivation talk aloud at a measured pace (p.203). Students number the seven events in sequence. Teacher reads the talk a second time; students check and adjust their ordering.

Teacher poses the three comprehension questions aloud (main step in soil preparation; weeks for seedlings; reason for drying). Students choose the correct option and answers are confirmed through a brief whole-class check.

Teacher models the silent-letter words — hymn, column, autumn, solemn, womb, tomb, bomb, climb — and students repeat each set aloud chorally then in pairs. Students then note which silent-letter pattern (silent 'n' with 'm'; silent 'b' with 'm') applies to each word.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening talk mirrors the poem's harvest theme — paddy cultivation is the real-world process behind the gratitude expressed in the hymn. Students commonly misorder 'puddling' and 'ploughing'; stress that the talk explicitly calls puddling 'the most important step in preparing the soil', which places it after ploughing. The silent-letter activity connects organically to the poem's own title word 'hymn', giving students an immediate anchor.
materials: Teacher's copy of the paddy-cultivation talk (p.203)

periods.activity_title: Harvest Dish Presentation and Farmer Gratitude Slogan

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.182): group presentation on a popular harvest festival dish from your region.
Let us write (p.183): draft a creative slogan of gratitude to farmers for the notice board.

time_bands.activity: Introduce both activities: the speaking task asks each group to present a harvest festival dish; the writing task asks each student to draft a slogan honouring farmers. Divide the class into groups of three or four.

Groups use the six provided prompts — dish name, regional variants, ingredients, preparation, serving style, special memory — to structure a brief oral presentation. Teacher circulates and guides groups who are unsure of the prompt sequence.

Two or three groups deliver their presentations to the class. After each, one classmate offers a single compliment and one question. Teacher notes confident vocabulary and pronunciation for brief feedback.

Students individually draft their farmer-gratitude slogan: they identify the main idea, choose simple language, and aim for conciseness. Students read their slogans aloud to a partner, revise if needed, and write the final version neatly on paper or in their notebooks.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked with the poem's devotional tone and harvest imagery, students now produce their own expressive language. Students who hesitate during presentations may be encouraged to begin by simply naming their dish and one ingredient — the prompts scaffold the rest. For the slogan, watch for attempts that are too long; model how to reduce 'Our farmers work hard every day so that we can eat' to a crisp, memorable phrase.
materials: Notebooks or chart paper for slogan drafting

periods.activity_title: Short-Answer Questions on the Poem and Millet Exploration Project

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.179): answer four short questions on rain, wealth, gladness, labours.
Let us explore (p.184): group activities on millets — cuisine connection, recipe collection, own recipe.

homework.task_brief: Let us explore (p.184): learn a harvest festival song from an elder and prepare to share.

time_bands.activity: Students re-read the poem silently, then answer four short questions in writing: why farmers hail the god of rain; what 'wealth of our valleys' refers to; why Earth is called 'source of manifold gladness'; and why everyone offers 'labours for tribute'. Answers are compared in pairs before class discussion.

Teacher introduces the Pearl Millet information on p.184. Groups of four discuss whether millets feature in their regional cuisine, citing specific dishes or ingredients they know. Brief group reports to the class follow.

Each group begins collecting or composing one millet recipe — drawing on what they shared — and drafts it in a structured format: name, ingredients, steps, serving suggestion. Groups share their draft recipe title and one distinctive ingredient with the class. Teacher assigns the harvest-song task as home research.

periods.teacher_notes: Having engaged with the poem's imagery of rain, grain, and earth throughout the chapter, students can now bring their own cultural knowledge to the short answers and the millet project. A common difficulty in the short questions is confusing 'wealth of our valleys' with abstract riches — direct students back to Varuna's stanza, where 'new-garnered and ripe' clarifies it is the freshly harvested grain. The millet recipe activity works best when groups include students from different culinary backgrounds; encourage them to compare ingredients across regional versions.

items.item_stem:
Read the lines on page 173 beginning “Lord of the lotus, lord of the harvest.”

Which statement correctly identifies the central idea of the first stanza of the poem?

A. The farmers thank Varuna for sending rain that nourished their crops.
B. The men’s voices thank Surya for his light and bounty that helped their harvest thrive.
C. All voices together praise Brahma as the source of all life and creation.
D. The women praise Prithvi for her fertile womb that brings their riches to life.

options.label: A
options.text: All voices together praise Brahma as the source of all life and creation.

options.label: B
options.text: The farmers thank Varuna for sending rain that nourished their crops.

options.label: C
options.text: The men’s voices thank Surya for his light and bounty that helped their harvest thrive.

options.label: D
options.text: The women praise Prithvi for her fertile womb that brings their riches to life.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has conflated the first and second stanzas, attributing Varuna’s rain to the opening stanza.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has skipped to the final stanza and missed the sequential address to individual deities.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has confused the men’s voices stanza with the women’s voices stanza addressed to Prithvi.

items.source_lo: Student identifies central ideas and structural organisation in a poem using close reading as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Four-stanza hymn addressing Surya, Varuna, Prithvi, and Brahma; harvest gratitude; choral voices.
items.item_stem: The final stanza of Harvest Hymn is sung by “All Voices” and addresses Brahma. Explain why the poet places this collective voice last, after the individual voices of men and women. What does the progression from separate voices to a single chorus suggest about the poem’s central theme?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Naidu places the collective chorus last to show that all human devotion — expressed by men praising Surya, women praising Prithvi — converges in a single act of worship directed at the universal creator, Brahma. The progression from separate voices to one chorus reinforces the poem’s central theme: the entire farming community, regardless of gender or role, is united in reverence and dependence on the divine forces that sustain life.

items.item_stem:
A teacher reads aloud the talk on paddy cultivation (p.203). After listening, arrange the following five steps of paddy cultivation in the correct order by numbering them 1 to 5.

(i) Threshing of grains
(ii) Puddling of land
(iii) Transplanting of seedlings
(iv) Milling of rice
(v) Ploughing of soil

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Ploughing of soil  2. Puddling of land  3. Transplanting of seedlings  4. Threshing of grains  5. Milling of rice.

items.source_lo: Student sequences information and retrieves key details from a listened informational talk as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Spoken talk on paddy cultivation: ploughing, puddling, transplanting, threshing, milling steps.
items.item_stem: In the talk on paddy cultivation, the speaker explains that drying the grains after threshing serves a specific purpose. State that purpose in your own words. Then explain what would likely happen to the harvested grain if this step were skipped.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Drying reduces the moisture content of the separated grains so they can be stored for longer periods or processed further through milling. If this step were skipped, the grains would retain excess moisture, making them prone to spoilage, mould, or difficulty in milling.

items.item_stem: Harvest Hymn celebrates the gratitude farmers feel toward nature at harvest time. Imagine you are presenting at a school assembly about a food dish traditionally prepared in your region during a harvest festival. Speak for about two minutes using the following points as a guide: what the dish is called and whether it has other regional names; the key ingredients and how they connect to the harvest; one special memory or ritual associated with preparing it. Give your own opinion on why such dishes matter to a community.

expected_elements: Names the dish and mentions at least one regional variant.
Links key ingredients to harvest or agricultural produce.
Describes one specific memory or cultural ritual clearly.
Gives a personal opinion with a supporting reason.

items.item_stem: Your school is putting up a display board titled ‘Those Who Feed Us.’ Write a short notice (40–60 words) for the board that thanks farmers for their work and invites students to learn more about where their food comes from. Your notice must include: a heading, a main message of gratitude, and one action students can take.

expected_elements: Includes a clear heading appropriate to a notice board.
Expresses genuine gratitude to farmers in simple language.
States one specific action students can take.
Stays within approximately 40–60 words; language is concise.

items.item_stem: Sarojini Naidu’s poem expresses the farming community’s gratitude to the forces of nature through song and garlands. Imagine you are a student who has just read Harvest Hymn. Write a short blog post (80–100 words) for your school’s online magazine in which you share what the poem made you feel about the relationship between farmers and nature, and why you think people today should remember that relationship.

expected_elements: Adopts an informal but thoughtful blog-post tone.
References at least one specific image or idea from the poem.
States a personal feeling or opinion about farmers and nature.
Explains relevance of the farmer-nature relationship today.

Column A|Column B
munificent|(i) beyond description or words
succour|(ii) brightness or glowing light

items.source_context: Farming implement names; synonyms for munificent, succour, radiance, ineffable; archaic words morrow, hither, yonder.
items.item_stem:
Harvest Hymn uses archaic language — words that were common in older English but are rarely used today. The following sentence uses three archaic words. Rewrite the sentence replacing each archaic word (shown in parentheses) with its modern equivalent, and then explain in one sentence how the meaning of the rewritten sentence stays the same.

“Come (hither) and look (yonder) at the fields, for on the (morrow) we shall begin the harvest.”

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Rewritten sentence: “Come here and look over there at the fields, for tomorrow we shall begin the harvest.” The meaning remains identical because ‘hither’, ‘yonder’ and ‘morrow’ are simply older forms of ‘here’, ‘over there’, and ‘tomorrow’ respectively, referring to the same locations and time.

items.source_context: Millets as traditional grains; regional cuisine connections; recipe creation; harvest festival cultural practices.
items.item_stem: The chapter mentions millets as a group of small-seeded grasses with high fibre and mineral content. Working in a group, find out whether millets are used in the cuisine of your region. Prepare a written report (one page) that includes: the name of at least one millet used locally, one dish made from it, and the occasion or meal it is typically served at. Share your report with the class.

expected_elements: Names at least one specific millet variety found in the region.
Describes one dish made from that millet with key ingredients.
States the occasion or meal context for the dish.
Report is clearly organised and written in complete sentences.

items.source_lo: Student connects a literary text to real-world cultural and agricultural knowledge through project-based inquiry as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Millets as traditional grains; regional cuisine connections; recipe creation; harvest festival cultural practices.
items.item_stem: Harvest Hymn celebrates the bond between farming communities and the natural world. As a group project, create a ‘Harvest Recipe Booklet’ that brings together traditional recipes using grains — including at least one millet recipe — associated with harvest festivals in your region or in other parts of India. For each recipe, write a two-sentence introduction explaining the cultural significance of that dish during the harvest season. Your booklet should include at least three recipes and a short group reflection (one paragraph) on what you learnt about the connection between food, farming, and culture.

expected_elements: Booklet contains at least three recipes, one using millets.
Each recipe includes a cultural significance introduction.
Group reflection connects food, farming, and harvest culture.
Presentation is organised, legible, and shows collaborative effort.
